newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: EBRD INTERESTED IN SLOVAK BANK PRIVATISATION.
newsitem.headline: EBRD INTERESTED IN SLOVAK BANK PRIVATISATION.

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) has expressed an interest to participate in the privatisation of Skia's banking sector, the finance ministry said.

"EBRD Vice-president Guy de Selliers has expressed the bank's interest in taking an active part in Slovak bank privatisation," ministry spokeswoman Zuzana Brutenicova told Reuters after talks between EBRD and finance ministry on Tuesday.
According to EBRD, the bank could play the "crucial role of a so-called stable shareholder participating in the development and strenghtening of a particular bank," she added.
She would not elaborate further. EBRD representatives were not available for comment.

The restructuring and privatisation of Slovakia's four major financial institutions -- banks VUB, IRB and Slovenska Sporitelna, and the largest insurer Slovenska Poistovna -- is considered crucial for further economic reform and acceptance of Slovakia to western economic structures.
The government has announced it will support banking sell-offs to large local companies, which are, in most cases the banks' major debtors.
The OECD recently criticised such plans, saying it would undermine the entire bank privatisation process, which in any case was postponed by parliament until the end of March 1997.

The EBRD is also scheduled to meet with the state privatisation agency, the National Property Fund (NPF), later on Tuesday, apparently to end protracted negotiations over the sale of the bank's stake in oil refiner Slovnaft.
The NPF declined to comment on the agenda of the meeting, but one fund official last week said the sale may be completed as early as this week.
The EBRD took a 10.5 percent stake in Slovnaft in 1995 when it bought half of the refiner's $113 million issue of global depositary receipts, which flopped on international markets.
The London-based development bank, set up to encourage free market reforms in post-communist Europe, effectively paid the 1,000 crowns ($32.09) per share face value.
But shortly afterwards, the NPF sold an additional 39 percent of Slovnaft to a management-led consortium called Slovintegra at an implied prices of just 156 crowns per share.
At the end of last year, the bank said it was wanted to leave Slovnaft, saying it "got burnt when it bought into it."
Since then both the fund and EBRD have said several times they were close to reaching a final decision on the sale, but no conclusion has yet been anounced.
